98d855fc19.q: What are examples of successful adaptive reuse projects that balance historic preservation with modern development in Portland?
98d855fc19.a: The Monument Hotel, developed by Jim Brady, is restoring a former bank building using historic tax credits and combining preserved elements like marble…
98d855fc19.e: Episode 77: Featuring Julie Gondzar, Director of Development, Greater Portland Landmarks
f: Portland has proven that historic tax credits and smart adaptive reuse can transform vacant bank buildings and residential properties into thriving modern spaces without sacrificing their character. The Monument Hotel and Safford House stand as tangible examples of this balance, each preserving original architectural details while meeting contemporary needs.
From Bank to Boutique Hotel: The Monument Hotel Story

Developer Jim Brady took on the challenge of converting a former bank building into the Monument Hotel, a project that demonstrates how historic tax credits unlock financial feasibility for preservation work. The restored structure retains striking original features—marble walls and intact structural elements—while incorporating modern hotel operations and guest amenities seamlessly into the preserved framework.

This approach is not incidental to the success; as Julie Gondzar explains in the episode , the combination of preserved historic elements with necessary modern updates shows developers that preservation and profitability are not opposing forces. Tax incentives make the numbers work without requiring the demolition that dominated Portland's urban renewal era in the 1960s and 70s.
Office Space with Character: The Safford House Transformation

At 93 High Street, the Safford House underwent a parallel transformation under the ownership of Woodhull, a company that chose modernization over demolition. The building was converted into office space while preserving original woodworking and built-in cabinetry that define the interior character. The project earned recognition through preservation awards, validating the market demand for office environments with authentic historic charm.

b9e7be1923.q: What misconceptions do developers hold about the barriers to historic preservation projects?
b9e7be1923.a: One of the biggest misconceptions is that there are heavy barriers that cannot be passed. Julie states that preservation should not be as scary as…
b9e7be1923.e: Episode 77: Featuring Julie Gondzar, Director of Development, Greater Portland Landmarks
f: The biggest misconception is that heavy, insurmountable barriers block preservation projects. Preservation is far less restrictive than developers often assume , and there are numerous creative solutions available. When people understand the real value of historic preservation, they can meaningfully alter and improve properties while protecting the elements that matter most.

Developers frequently overestimate the constraints they'll face when working with historic buildings. This fear often stems from outdated assumptions about preservation rules and a lack of familiarity with how modern preservation actually works. Julie Gondzar, Director of Development at Greater Portland Landmarks, emphasizes that preservation should not be as scary as it appears .

The reality is that flexibility and creativity exist within preservation frameworks . Many projects that initially seem impossible become feasible once developers sit down with preservation professionals and understand what truly must be preserved versus what can be modified. The distinction matters enormously—and it's often a difference between a project's success and its abandonment.

In practice, this means developers can improve building systems, update interiors, add modern amenities, and even expand or reconfigure spaces, provided they preserve the character-defining features that give the building its historic significance. The key is early collaboration. As Gondzar discusses in this episode , Greater Portland Landmarks has shifted from confrontational approaches to proactive partnerships with developers, recognizing that shared goals produce better outcomes.
From Fear to Opportunity

Many developers approach historic buildings with the assumption that preservation requirements will cripple their project timeline, budget, or vision. This misconception creates an unnecessary barrier that often exists primarily in the developer's mind, not in the actual preservation guidelines. When barriers are real, they are almost always surmountable through dialogue and creative problem-solving.

2c003ad491.q: What is the role and public access situation of the Portland Observatory on Munjoy Hill?
2c003ad491.a: Greater Portland Landmarks is the steward of the Portland Observatory, which is owned by the City of Portland. The observatory is open May through October…
2c003ad491.e: Episode 77: Featuring Julie Gondzar, Director of Development, Greater Portland Landmarks
f: Greater Portland Landmarks serves as steward of the Portland Observatory , which is owned by the City of Portland. The building is open to the public from May through October and hosts guided tours attracting thousands of visitors annually from around the world.
From Signal Tower to Public Heritage Site

The Portland Observatory began its life with a practical maritime purpose. The structure originally functioned as a signal tower where flags were raised to alert the community about incoming ships , reflecting Portland's deep connection to its working waterfront and ocean commerce. This historic role ties directly to the preservation mission that brought Julie Gondzar to Greater Portland Landmarks.

Today, the experience visitors encounter has been shaped by careful restoration and interpretation. Educational displays throughout the building explain its original history and the reconstructions undertaken to preserve it for future generations. As Gondzar notes in the episode , these efforts reflect Greater Portland Landmarks' commitment to making historic structures accessible and meaningful to the public.

The seasonal operation—May through October—aligns with visitor demand and the organizational capacity of Greater Portland Landmarks, which manages multiple properties and preservation initiatives across the region. The fact that thousands of visitors arrive annually from across the globe underscores the Observatory's significance as both a local landmark and an international attraction.

0a40ee3f5a.q: What factors drive professionals to transition from business ownership in the private sector to nonprofit leadership roles?
0a40ee3f5a.a: Julie sought a new career path after years in business and was anxious to step into the nonprofit world. Her background naturally led her to development…
0a40ee3f5a.e: Episode 77: Featuring Julie Gondzar, Director of Development, Greater Portland Landmarks
f: The shift from private business ownership to nonprofit leadership is typically driven by a desire for deeper community connection, family proximity, and alignment with a personal mission. For Julie Gondzar, that meant leaving her thriving specialty coffee roastery in Wyoming to return to New England and support historic preservation efforts—a move anchored in family, legacy, and the opportunity to build relationships at a different scale.

Julie spent 18 years of her childhood coming to Scarborough and Portland, and that deep connection to New England was a primary motivator for the geographic move back to Maine. The decision wasn't solely about nostalgia; it was about creating a tangible sense of place for herself, her husband, and their daughter. Moving back to Maine meant proximity to family and the ability to put down roots in a real community rather than continuing to build a business in isolation.

Beyond family, Julie recognized that her background and skillset naturally translated to nonprofit development work . She had spent years building Snowy Elk Coffee Company—an award-winning specialty roastery she co-founded with her husband in 2017—where she handled sales, marketing, and business development. That experience in relationship-building, brand development, and scaling operations prepared her for the fundraising and stakeholder engagement required in the nonprofit sector, as detailed in the episode .

The final piece was a personal commitment to historic preservation in southern Maine. Julie's passion for preserving Portland's marine culture, working ports, and historic architecture gave her mission-driven work a clear purpose. She wasn't just looking for a new job; she was seeking alignment between her daily work and her values—something that required stepping out of the private sector into a cause she genuinely believed in.
"Success ultimately comes from collaboration. I believe that if you want a good result at the end of the day, collaboration is key."

Julie Gondzar — Director of Development, Greater Portland Landmarks. Julie joined Greater Portland Landmarks in January 2025 after relocating from Wyoming, where she had co-founded Snowy Elk Coffee Company and held extensive experience in both public and private sectors. Originally from New England, she holds a master's degree from Plymouth State University and brings a background in science, water management, and business development to her work championing historic preservation in Portland.

a17f4b5ca4.q: How should preservation organizations balance advocacy with collaboration when engaging developers on historic buildings?
a17f4b5ca4.a: Greater Portland Landmarks has shifted from being confrontational to being proactive and collaborative. The organization now seeks to get a seat at the…
a17f4b5ca4.e: Episode 77: Featuring Julie Gondzar, Director of Development, Greater Portland Landmarks
f: Successful preservation requires shifting from confrontation to proactive collaboration —getting a seat at the table early in the development process rather than opposing plans after they're made. Greater Portland Landmarks has found that serving as a resource for developers, while maintaining readiness to advocate firmly when necessary, produces better outcomes than adversarial approaches.
From Opposition to Partnership

Greater Portland Landmarks has evolved its strategy over time, moving away from a purely confrontational stance toward developers. The shift reflects a strategic recognition that preservation battles are won not by blocking projects, but by shaping them from within. Being part of the planning process from the start allows preservation groups to influence decisions while developers still have flexibility to integrate historic sensitivity into their vision.

This proactive approach means engaging developers as partners, not adversaries. Rather than waiting for project announcements and then mobilizing opposition, preservation organizations now seek opportunities to offer expertise, guidance, and solutions that align both historic character and development goals.
Knowing When to Push Back

Collaboration does not mean accepting every proposal without question. Advocacy groups must remain willing to draw a line when core preservation values are at stake. The difference lies in timing and tone: by building relationships and demonstrating good faith through earlier cooperation, organizations gain credibility and influence when they do choose to oppose something.

f: Rely's AI-powered software automates the entire audit process—lease files, utilities, contracts, and financial data—for apartment complexes, compressing what typically takes 60 to 90 days of due diligence into completion within a single day once data is received. This automation is powered by AI's ability to read, scan, organize, and search information at scale, a capability that would have been impossible without current machine learning technologies.
The Four-Pillar Automation Framework

Rely's platform handles four critical audit categories simultaneously. The software processes lease files to verify tenant agreements, utility audits to reconcile consumption and billing, contract audits to identify obligations and risks, and financial audits to validate property economics. Rather than having human auditors spend weeks manually reviewing documents, the AI engine ingests all data at once and surfaces findings in structured, actionable reports.

As George Matelich explains in the episode , this consolidation eliminates the sequential bottleneck that has defined the traditional due diligence process. Each audit phase typically required different teams and multiple review cycles, creating natural delays. Automation collapses that timeline because document processing happens in parallel , not in series.
Why Speed Matters in Portfolio Churn

The real estate industry faces a structural pressure that makes faster due diligence critical: properties flip in and out of managed portfolios at a rate of approximately 30% per year. This means a firm managing a portfolio must continuously evaluate new acquisitions while assets shift hands or change operators.
